hints: Use the form A/(3a+2x)+B/(2a−x), since both denominator factors are linear.
Clear denominators and either compare coefficients of x and a or substitute values that zero one factor.
Insert both constants and recombine the fractions to check the numerator 3a−5x.
walkthrough:
Set up the partial fraction decomposition for linear distinct factors:
$$\dfrac{3a - 5x}{(3a + 2x)(2a - x)} = \dfrac{A}{3a + 2x} + \dfrac{B}{2a - x}$$

Clear denominators by multiplying by $(3a + 2x)(2a - x)$:
$$3a - 5x = A(2a - x) + B(3a + 2x)$$

Substitute $x = 2a$ to eliminate $A$:
$$3a - 5(2a) = A(0) + B(3a + 2(2a))$$
$$3a - 10a = B(3a + 4a)$$
$$-7a = 7a B \implies B = -1$$

Substitute $x = -\dfrac{3a}{2}$ to eliminate $B$:
$$3a - 5\left(-\dfrac{3a}{2}\right) = A\left(2a - \left(-\dfrac{3a}{2}\right)\right) + B(0)$$
$$3a + \dfrac{15a}{2} = A\left(2a + \dfrac{3a}{2}\right)$$
$$\dfrac{21a}{2} = \dfrac{7a}{2}A \implies 21 = 7A \implies A = 3$$

hints: Rewrite each fraction from part (a) as a constant times (1+u)^(−1).
Expand 1/(3a+2x) using u=2x/(3a), and 1/(2a−x) using u=−x/(2a), through x².
Apply the coefficients from part (a), combine like powers of x, and simplify every power of a.
walkthrough:
Rewrite the first partial fraction into standard binomial form:
$$\dfrac{3}{3a + 2x} = \dfrac{3}{3a\left(1 + \dfrac{2x}{3a}\right)} = \dfrac{1}{a}\left(1 + \dfrac{2x}{3a}\right)^{-1}$$

Rewrite and expand the second partial fraction:
$$-\dfrac{1}{2a - x} = -\dfrac{1}{2a\left(1 - \dfrac{x}{2a}\right)} = -\dfrac{1}{2a}\left(1 - \dfrac{x}{2a}\right)^{-1}$$
$$-\dfrac{1}{2a}\left[1 + \dfrac{x}{2a} + \left(\dfrac{x}{2a}\right)^2\right] = -\dfrac{1}{2a}\left[1 + \dfrac{1}{2a}x + \dfrac{1}{4a^2}x^2\right] = -\dfrac{1}{2a} - \dfrac{1}{4a^2}x - \dfrac{1}{8a^3}x^2$$

Combine the two series expansions term-by-term:
$$\text{Constant: } \dfrac{1}{a} - \dfrac{1}{2a} = \dfrac{1}{2a}$$
$$\text{Term in } x: \left(-\dfrac{2}{3a^2} - \dfrac{1}{4a^2}\right)x = -\left(\dfrac{8 + 3}{12}\right)\dfrac{1}{a^2}x = -\dfrac{11}{12a^2}x$$
$$\text{Term in } x^2: \left(\dfrac{4}{9a^3} - \dfrac{1}{8a^3}\right)x^2 = \left(\dfrac{32 - 9}{72}\right)\dfrac{1}{a^3}x^2 = \dfrac{23}{72a^3}x^2$$

hints: Apply this separately to |2x/(3a)|<1 and |x/(2a)|<1, remembering a>0.
The combined expansion is valid on the intersection of the two open intervals; state the more restrictive condition.
walkthrough:
Find the validity condition for the first expansion $\left(1 + \dfrac{2x}{3a}\right)^{-1}$:
$$\left| \dfrac{2x}{3a} \right| < 1 \implies \dfrac{2}{3a}|x| < 1 \implies |x| < \dfrac{3a}{2}$$

Find the validity condition for the second expansion $\left(1 - \dfrac{x}{2a}\right)^{-1}$:
$$\left| -\dfrac{x}{2a} \right| < 1 \implies \dfrac{1}{2a}|x| < 1 \implies |x| < 2a$$

Determine the overall validity by taking the intersection of the two ranges:
$$\text{Since } \dfrac{3a}{2} = 1.5a < 2a, \text{ the more restrictive condition is:}$$
$$|x| < \dfrac{3a}{2} \quad \left(\text{or } -\dfrac{3a}{2} < x < \dfrac{3a}{2}\right)$$
